title: Do you ever feel hesitant about using AI assistance in game development?
author: Walter-Brown-
selftext:
I'm curious how other indie developers feel about using AI tools while making their games.

I'm a solo developer, and obviously, I don't have the skills to do everything myself. I'm still learning game development, and I use AI assistance for things like coding, debugging, and figuring out problems I wouldn't know how to approach otherwise.

But sometimes I feel a little weird about it. I worry that if people find out how much AI assistance went into making my game, they won't be as impressed. Almost as if the achievement becomes less meaningful because I didn't figure everything out on my own.

At the same time, being a solo developer means wearing a lot of hats. I can't realistically be an expert programmer, artist, designer, animator, and everything else.

I know AI is a tool, but I still wonder where the line is between using it to bring your ideas to life and relying on it too much.

comments.author: orblabs
comments.body:
I started my career in game dev 20 years ago with the first public beta of Unity, i have been around the first years, then the later ones. Up until not long ago, all the crap and gatekeeping from the game dev community towards LLMs,  was , for the very same reasons, targeted towards unity developers. We where not real programmers as unity script (and later  c#) where not "real" programming languages and the games we made where not real games as they where made with a toy app not a real game engine you had to build with each change. It wasn't only devs altho, there was also the "unity look" problem which is comparable to one prompt LLM game creations, unpolished, and users feel it. Unity could always (more or less) output stunning graphics, but most people would stick to the defaults and most games would look the same).

What i am trying to say is that.. it is normal, the old guard in development or any other field, will absolutely hate the new tools they don't understand or don't want to understand, they have worked in other ways all their lives, it is understandable.  
The only thing you will have to worry is the quality of what reaches your players, the tools that got you there are imo irrelevant, just avoid the "slop" feel and put passion into your project.  
Best luck !

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
Feeling a bit weird about it is pretty normal, but players mostly care whether the game is good, and the decisions that make it good are still yours: what to build, what to cut, what feels right, and when something isn't fun yet.

A line that's worked for a lot of solo devs: use AI for things you could eventually learn but don't have time for, and make sure you understand what ships. If it writes a system, ask it to explain it until you could change it yourself. Then you're learning on the job, not just outsourcing. And being upfront about it on your store page usually lands better than people expect, since the people who'd be put off would find out anyway.

comments.author: zayelion
comments.body: Its more so a worry about dependence on the tool, and it being the infrastructure/substrate of the process rather than just the tool. If I repeat an action I try to find a way to turn that into a script. The pricing of the models jumps all over the place and I need to be able to understand my own code and processes. So creating a script crystalizes this. Sometimes it teaches me to go and find better local models.
